title: CHOROIDAL TUMOURS: A Clinical Masterclass
summary: An exhaustive guide to the diagnosis, differential diagnosis, investigation, and multi-modal treatment of choroidal melanoma and simulating lesions. This poster details clinical signs, histopathological features, and modern genetic prognostic indicators.

sections.title: Diagnosis and Initial Presentation
content: Symptoms are often absent, with a tumour detected by chance on routine fundus examination.
A range of visual disturbance can occur depending on tumour characteristics.
Signs: A solitary elevated subretinal grey-brown (Fig. 20.26A) or rarely amelanotic (Fig. 20.26B) dome-shaped mass.
Diffuse infiltration is uncommon.
About 60% are located within 3 mm of the optic disc (Fig. 20.26C) or fovea.
Clumps of overlying orange pigment are common (Fig. 20.26D).

sections.title: Advanced Clinical Signs
content: Breakthrough: If the tumour breaks through Bruch membrane it acquires a ‘collar stud’ appearance (see Fig. 20.25C and Fig. 20.28C).
Associated haemorrhage and subretinal fluid (Fig. 20.26E) are common.
Exudative retinal detachment (Fig. 20.26F) may result from subretinal fluid, which can mask the underlying lesion.
Other signs: Sentinel vessels (Fig. 20.27), choroidal folds, inflammation, rubeosis iridis, secondary glaucoma and cataract.

rows: Usually exhibits numerous surface drusen, without serous retinal detachment and little if any orange pigment.
Deeply pigmented and usually located at the optic disc.
Flat, often grey-black; has a well-defined margin with lacunae.
In subretinal or suprachoroidal space (e.g., from choroidal neovascularization or retinal artery macroaneurysm).
Smooth surface, light brown colour, indistinct margins, extensive retinal detachment; often a past history of malignancy.
Typically posterior, pink, dome-shaped with a smooth surface.
Often associated with exudative retinal detachment.
Presents with large elevated lesion; unlike melanoma, pain is a common feature.
Eccentrically located (temporal pre-equatorial), associated with exudate and fresh haemorrhage (rare in melanoma).
Small, smooth, brown, dome-shaped lesion that disappears with pressure on the eye.
Tightly arranged fusiform cells with indistinct cell membranes and slender or plump oval nuclei.
Large pleomorphic cells with distinct cell membranes, large vesicular nuclei with prominent nucleoli, and abundant cytoplasm.

sections.title: Diagnostic Investigations (Imaging)
content: Examination: Sufficient for diagnosis in the majority of cases.

Fluorescein Angiography (FA): Limited diagnostic value; no pathognomonic pattern. Shows intrinsic ‘dual’ circulation (Fig. 20.28A), mottled fluorescence (arteriovenous phase), late diffuse leakage and staining.

Ultrasound: Measures dimensions and detects tumours through opaque media/exudative detachment. Shows internal homogeneity, low to medium reflectivity, choroidal excavation (Fig. 20.28B), and orbital shadowing.
Acoustic Hollowing: A basal acoustically quiet zone due to greater tissue homogeneity in this region.
Collar Stud (US): Configuration (Fig. 20.28C) is almost pathognomonic when present.
FAF: Intense diffuse or confluent hyperautofluorescence is a useful indicator of melanoma.
OCT: Measures dimensions and demonstrates subretinal fluid/secondary retinal changes overlying the lesion.
ICGA: Usually shows hypofluorescence throughout; provides more information than FA about tumour extent due to lower RPE interference.
MRI: Useful for extraocular extension (Fig. 20.28D) and differential diagnosis.

sections.title: Biopsy and Advanced Pathology
content: Biopsy: Used when diagnosis is not established by non-invasive methods. Performed via fine needle or 25-gauge vitrectomy system (larger sample).
Immunocytochemistry (PAX8): Distinguishes tumours. Melanoma and melanocytoma are PAX8-negative; pigmented adenocarcinomas are PAX8-positive.

content.explanation: Loss of one copy of chromosome 3 (M3) and changes in chromosome 8 (i8q) strongly correlate with poor outcome, especially when occurring together. Metastasis occurs almost exclusively with certain genetic profiles.

sections.title: Prognostic Resources
content: The Liverpool Uveal Melanoma Prognosticator is an online resource combining anatomic, genetic, and histopathological data to determine prognosis for life.
Reduced surveillance can be adopted for patients with a low-risk genetic profile.

sections.title: Systemic Investigation Protocol
content: Step 1: Detect metastatic spread (primary focus on liver).
Step 2: Liver function testing and ultrasonography (mainstays).
Step 3: Chest radiography (rarely shows lung secondaries without liver disease).
Step 4: Consider whole-body PET/CT (Greater sensitivity for extrahepatic lesions, but high ionizing radiation dose).

sections.title: Treatment Principles
content: Objective: Avoid a painful/unsightly eye while conserving useful vision.
Survival: Influence of ocular treatment on survival is not yet defined, though smaller earlier tumours may have lower risk of metastasis.
Management: Individualized based on tumour characteristics (apical height, basal diameter) and patient factors (health, age, preferences, fellow eye).

rows: Tumours < 20mm basal diameter and < 10mm thick. Plaque sutured to sclera for several days. Regression starts 1–2 months post-treatment.
Cataract, papillopathy, disc neovascularization, radiation retinopathy, 'toxic tumour syndrome'.
Used for large or posterior tumours unsuitable for brachytherapy. Targeting aided by tantalum markers. Survival comparable to brachytherapy.
Lashes loss, eyelid depigmentation, keratitis, and intraocular complications similar to brachytherapy.
Multiple collimated beams (concurrent or sequential) delivering high dose only to the tumour.
Effective, but may have a comparatively high complication rate.

sections.title: Laser and Surgical Therapies
content: Transpupillary thermotherapy (TTT): Uses infrared laser for hyperthermia (not coagulation). For small tumours when radiotherapy is inappropriate or for vision-threatening exudation. Tumour disappears to leave bare sclera.
TTT Complications: Retinal traction, tears, rhegmatogenous detachment, vascular occlusion, neovascularization. Local recurrence common in thick, amelanotic, or disc-margin tumours.
Trans-scleral choroidectomy: Technically difficult. For tumours > 16mm in diameter too thick for radiotherapy. Complications: Detachment, hypotony, wound dehiscence, recurrence.
Light-activated AU-011: Novel treatment for small melanomas (2–3.4 mm). Nano-particles from HPV + infrared dye injected into vitreous; activated by infrared light to cause necrosis.

sections.title: Enucleation: Removal of the Eye
content: Large tumour size
Optic disc invasion
Extensive involvement of ciliary body or angle
Irreversible loss of useful vision
Poor motivation to keep the eye
Critical: Must perform ophthalmoscopy after surgical draping to ensure correct eye is removed.

sections.title: Metastatic Disease Management
content: No standard treatment for metastatic disease exists.
Tebentafusc: Immunotherapy drug that can modestly increase survival in some patients.
Note: Cutaneous melanoma checkpoint inhibitors are NOT effective against uveal melanoma.
Systemic chemotherapy has NOT been shown to benefit cases without evidence of metastatic spread.
